quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Demonstrative 'this' with a singular subject
quests.sentenceWithBlank: This charger ___ my phone fully in an hour.
quests.completedSentence: This charger charges my phone fully in an hour.
quests.grammarRule: Demonstrative 'this' with a singular subject
quests.ruleExplanation: 'This charger' is singular (one item), so the verb takes the -s ending: 'charges'. The demonstrative 'this' always signals a singular noun.
quests.nativeTip: 'This' points to one singular item - check what that means for the verb.
quests.example: This charger charges my phone fully in an hour.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Demonstrative 'these' with a plural subject
quests.sentenceWithBlank: These chargers ___ multiple devices at once.
quests.completedSentence: These chargers charge multiple devices at once.
quests.grammarRule: Demonstrative 'these' with a plural subject
quests.ruleExplanation: 'These chargers' is plural, since 'these' signals more than one item. Plural subjects take the base verb form: 'charge'.
quests.nativeTip: 'These' always points to more than one thing.
quests.example: These chargers charge multiple devices at once.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Demonstrative 'that' with a singular subject
quests.sentenceWithBlank: That printer in the corner ___ paper constantly.
quests.completedSentence: That printer in the corner jams paper constantly.
quests.grammarRule: Demonstrative 'that' with a singular subject
quests.ruleExplanation: The subject is 'that printer', a singular noun; 'in the corner' just adds detail. Singular subjects need -s: 'jams'.
quests.nativeTip: Look past the extra description ('in the corner') to find the real subject.
quests.example: That printer in the corner jams paper constantly.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Possessive noun phrase - agreement with the head noun, not the possessor
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The doctor's office ___ new patients on Mondays.
quests.completedSentence: The doctor's office accepts new patients on Mondays.
quests.grammarRule: Possessive noun phrase - agreement with the head noun, not the possessor
quests.ruleExplanation: The grammatical subject is 'office', not 'doctor'; the possessive 'doctor's' just modifies it. Since 'office' is singular, the verb takes -s: 'accepts'.
quests.nativeTip: The apostrophe-s belongs to 'doctor', but the real subject of the sentence is what follows it.
quests.example: The doctor's office accepts new patients on Mondays.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Possessive noun phrase - agreement with the head noun, not the possessor
quests.sentenceWithBlank: My parents' house ___ near the coast.
quests.completedSentence: My parents' house sits near the coast.
quests.grammarRule: Possessive noun phrase - agreement with the head noun, not the possessor
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Parents'' is possessive and plural, but the head noun is 'house', which is singular. The verb agrees with 'house': 'sits'.
quests.nativeTip: Even though 'parents' is plural, check what noun the sentence is actually about.
quests.example: My parents' house sits near the coast.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Possessive noun phrase - agreement with the head noun, not the possessor
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The company's policies ___ every year.
quests.completedSentence: The company's policies change every year.
quests.grammarRule: Possessive noun phrase - agreement with the head noun, not the possessor
quests.ruleExplanation: The head noun here is 'policies', a plural noun, even though 'company's' looks singular. Plural head nouns take the base verb form: 'change'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Company's' is singular, but look at the noun it's describing before choosing the verb.
quests.example: The company's policies change every year.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Auxiliary 'do/does' agreement with the subject in questions
quests.sentenceWithBlank: ___ your brother speak French fluently?
quests.completedSentence: Does your brother speak French fluently?
quests.grammarRule: Auxiliary 'do/does' agreement with the subject in questions
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Your brother' is singular, so the question needs 'does': 'Does your brother speak French fluently?' 'Do' would only work with a plural subject or with I/you.
quests.nativeTip: Check whether the subject after the blank is singular or plural before choosing the auxiliary.
quests.example: Does your brother speak French fluently?

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Auxiliary 'do/does' agreement with the subject in questions
quests.sentenceWithBlank: ___ your parents celebrate any special holidays?
quests.completedSentence: Do your parents celebrate any special holidays?
quests.grammarRule: Auxiliary 'do/does' agreement with the subject in questions
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Your parents' is plural, so the question uses 'do': 'Do your parents celebrate...?' 'Does' is reserved for singular subjects.
quests.nativeTip: 'Parents' is plural - which auxiliary matches that?
quests.example: Do your parents celebrate any special holidays?

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Auxiliary 'do/does' agreement in negative sentences
quests.sentenceWithBlank: He ___ not usually check his messages after work.
quests.completedSentence: He does not usually check his messages after work.
quests.grammarRule: Auxiliary 'do/does' agreement in negative sentences
quests.ruleExplanation: 'He' is singular, so the negative form needs 'does': 'does not check'. 'Do not' would only fit a plural subject or I/you/we/they.
quests.nativeTip: This is a negative sentence - the auxiliary still has to agree with 'he'.
quests.example: He does not usually check his messages after work.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: 'have/has' agreement in the simple present
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The clinic ___ a new dentist starting next week.
quests.completedSentence: The clinic has a new dentist starting next week.
quests.grammarRule: 'have/has' agreement in the simple present
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The clinic' is singular, so the verb is 'has'. 'Have' is reserved for plural subjects and for I/you/we/they.
quests.nativeTip: Decide if the subject is one place or more than one before picking 'have' or 'has'.
quests.example: The clinic has a new dentist starting next week.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: 'have/has' agreement in the simple present
quests.sentenceWithBlank: Most apartments in this building ___ a small balcony.
quests.completedSentence: Most apartments in this building have a small balcony.
quests.grammarRule: 'have/has' agreement in the simple present
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Most apartments' is plural, so the verb is 'have'. 'Has' would incorrectly suggest a single apartment.
quests.nativeTip: 'Apartments' names more than one unit - which form matches that?
quests.example: Most apartments in this building have a small balcony.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: 'have' with the first-person pronoun 'I'
quests.sentenceWithBlank: I ___ a dentist appointment this afternoon.
quests.completedSentence: I have a dentist appointment this afternoon.
quests.grammarRule: 'have' with the first-person pronoun 'I'
quests.ruleExplanation: Even though 'I' refers to one person, it never takes 'has'. The pronoun 'I' always pairs with 'have', just like 'we', 'you', and 'they'.
quests.nativeTip: 'I' is a special case - it doesn't follow the usual he/she/it pattern.
quests.example: I have a dentist appointment this afternoon.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: 'be' verb agreement (is/are) in the simple present
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The bridge ___ closed for repairs this week.
quests.completedSentence: The bridge is closed for repairs this week.
quests.grammarRule: 'be' verb agreement (is/are) in the simple present
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The bridge' is singular, so it pairs with 'is'. 'Are' is used only with plural subjects or with 'you/we/they'.
quests.nativeTip: One bridge is singular - which form of 'be' matches that?
quests.example: The bridge is closed for repairs this week.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: 'be' verb agreement (is/are) in the simple present
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The results ___ available on the website now.
quests.completedSentence: The results are available on the website now.
quests.grammarRule: 'be' verb agreement (is/are) in the simple present
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The results' is plural, so the verb is 'are'. 'Is' would only be correct with a singular subject.
quests.nativeTip: 'Results' already looks plural - which 'be' form fits?
quests.example: The results are available on the website now.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: 'be' verb agreement with the pronoun 'I'
quests.sentenceWithBlank: I ___ excited about the new project.
quests.completedSentence: I am excited about the new project.
quests.grammarRule: 'be' verb agreement with the pronoun 'I'
quests.ruleExplanation: The pronoun 'I' always pairs with 'am', a unique form used only with the first-person singular subject.
quests.nativeTip: 'I' takes its own special form of 'be' - not 'is' and not 'are'.
quests.example: I am excited about the new project.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Base verb form after the auxiliary 'do/does'
quests.sentenceWithBlank: Does the team ___ enough players for Saturday's match?
quests.completedSentence: Does the team have enough players for Saturday's match?
quests.grammarRule: Base verb form after the auxiliary 'do/does'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Does' already carries the singular agreement, so the following verb stays in its base form: 'have', not 'has'. This is a common trap when 'does' or 'do' introduces the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Once 'does' appears, the main verb goes back to its base form - no extra -s needed.
quests.example: Does the team have enough players for Saturday's match?

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Base verb form after the auxiliary 'do/does'
quests.sentenceWithBlank: Do the printers on this floor ___ enough paper?
quests.completedSentence: Do the printers on this floor have enough paper?
quests.grammarRule: Base verb form after the auxiliary 'do/does'
quests.ruleExplanation: Whether the subject is singular or plural, once 'do' or 'does' appears, the following verb stays in the base form. Here it's 'have', not 'has'.
quests.nativeTip: After 'do', the main verb never takes -s, no matter the subject.
quests.example: Do the printers on this floor have enough paper?

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Base verb form after the negative auxiliary 'doesn't'
quests.sentenceWithBlank: She doesn't ___ time to finish the report today.
quests.completedSentence: She doesn't have time to finish the report today.
quests.grammarRule: Base verb form after the negative auxiliary 'doesn't'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Doesn't' (does not) already signals third-person singular agreement, so the verb that follows is the base form: 'have', never 'has'.
quests.nativeTip: The auxiliary 'doesn't' already shows the agreement - the verb after it stays in its base form.
quests.example: She doesn't have time to finish the report today.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Locating the subject when a phrase comes before it
quests.sentenceWithBlank: Every weekend, my uncle ___ fishing at the lake.
quests.completedSentence: Every weekend, my uncle goes fishing at the lake.
quests.grammarRule: Locating the subject when a phrase comes before it
quests.ruleExplanation: The phrase 'every weekend' just sets the time; the real subject is 'my uncle', which is singular. Singular subjects need -s: 'goes'.
quests.nativeTip: Skip past the introductory phrase and find who performs the action.
quests.example: Every weekend, my uncle goes fishing at the lake.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Locating the subject when a phrase comes before it
quests.sentenceWithBlank: In most large cities, public transportation ___ crowded during rush hour.
quests.completedSentence: In most large cities, public transportation becomes crowded during rush hour.
quests.grammarRule: Locating the subject when a phrase comes before it
quests.ruleExplanation: 'In most large cities' is an introductory phrase; the subject is 'public transportation', which is treated as singular. The verb takes -s: 'becomes'.
quests.nativeTip: The opening phrase names a place, not the subject - keep looking.
quests.example: In most large cities, public transportation becomes crowded during rush hour.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Locating the subject when a phrase comes before it
quests.sentenceWithBlank: Once a month, the book club members ___ a new novel.
quests.completedSentence: Once a month, the book club members discuss a new novel.
quests.grammarRule: Locating the subject when a phrase comes before it
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Once a month' introduces the sentence, but the subject is 'the book club members', which is plural. Plural subjects take the base form: 'discuss'.
quests.nativeTip: The time phrase at the start isn't the subject - look for who actually does the discussing.
quests.example: Once a month, the book club members discuss a new novel.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Possessive noun phrase - agreement with the head noun
quests.sentenceWithBlank: This student's essay ___ several strong arguments.
quests.completedSentence: This student's essay contains several strong arguments.
quests.grammarRule: Possessive noun phrase - agreement with the head noun
quests.ruleExplanation: The subject is 'essay', a singular noun modified by the possessive 'this student's'. Singular subjects take -s: 'contains'.
quests.nativeTip: The possessive 'student's' isn't the subject - find the noun it's attached to.
quests.example: This student's essay contains several strong arguments.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Possessive noun phrase - agreement with the head noun
quests.sentenceWithBlank: Those employees' schedules ___ every two weeks.
quests.completedSentence: Those employees' schedules change every two weeks.
quests.grammarRule: Possessive noun phrase - agreement with the head noun
quests.ruleExplanation: The head noun is 'schedules', which is plural, so the verb stays in the base form: 'change', not 'changes'.
quests.nativeTip: Look at what comes after the possessive to find the true subject.
quests.example: Those employees' schedules change every two weeks.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Possessive noun phrase - agreement with the head noun
quests.sentenceWithBlank: That manager's decisions ___ the whole department.
quests.completedSentence: That manager's decisions affect the whole department.
quests.grammarRule: Possessive noun phrase - agreement with the head noun
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Decisions' is the plural head noun, so the verb takes the base form: 'affect', not 'affects'.
quests.nativeTip: Identify whether the noun right before the verb is singular or plural.
quests.example: That manager's decisions affect the whole department.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: 'be' verb agreement (is/are) in questions
quests.sentenceWithBlank: ___ the store still open at this hour?
quests.completedSentence: Is the store still open at this hour?
quests.grammarRule: 'be' verb agreement (is/are) in questions
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The store' is singular, so the question uses 'is': 'Is the store still open...?'
quests.nativeTip: Check if 'the store' is singular or plural before choosing 'is' or 'are'.
quests.example: Is the store still open at this hour?

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: 'be' verb agreement (is/are) in questions
quests.sentenceWithBlank: ___ the new regulations already in effect?
quests.completedSentence: Are the new regulations already in effect?
quests.grammarRule: 'be' verb agreement (is/are) in questions
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The new regulations' is plural, so the question uses 'are': 'Are the new regulations already in effect?'
quests.nativeTip: 'Regulations' is already plural in form - which question word matches?
quests.example: Are the new regulations already in effect?

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: 'be' verb agreement (is/are) in questions
quests.sentenceWithBlank: ___ we allowed to bring guests to the event?
quests.completedSentence: Are we allowed to bring guests to the event?
quests.grammarRule: 'be' verb agreement (is/are) in questions
quests.ruleExplanation: 'We' is a plural pronoun, so the question form uses 'are': 'Are we allowed...?'
quests.nativeTip: 'We' is always plural, no matter the situation.
quests.example: Are we allowed to bring guests to the event?

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Demonstrative 'these' with a plural subject
quests.sentenceWithBlank: These instructions ___ confusing to new employees.
quests.completedSentence: These instructions seem confusing to new employees.
quests.grammarRule: Demonstrative 'these' with a plural subject
quests.ruleExplanation: 'These instructions' is plural because of 'these', so the verb takes the base form: 'seem'.
quests.nativeTip: Bring back the demonstrative rule: 'these' always signals a plural subject.
quests.example: These instructions seem confusing to new employees.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Auxiliary 'do/does' agreement with the subject in questions
quests.sentenceWithBlank: ___ your sister have a car, or does she take the bus?
quests.completedSentence: Does your sister have a car, or does she take the bus?
quests.grammarRule: Auxiliary 'do/does' agreement with the subject in questions
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Your sister' is singular, so the question needs 'does': 'Does your sister have a car...?'
quests.nativeTip: Recall the do/does rule from earlier in this stage.
quests.example: Does your sister have a car, or does she take the bus?

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: 'be' verb agreement with a possessive noun phrase subject
quests.sentenceWithBlank: My coworker's ideas ___ always practical and easy to apply.
quests.completedSentence: My coworker's ideas are always practical and easy to apply.
quests.grammarRule: 'be' verb agreement with a possessive noun phrase subject
quests.ruleExplanation: The subject is 'ideas' (plural), not 'coworker's'. Plural subjects pair with 'are', so 'are always practical' is correct.
quests.nativeTip: Combine two skills: find the head noun, then pick the right form of 'be'.
quests.example: My coworker's ideas are always practical and easy to apply.
